- Overestimate prices after recent spikes, especially when sentiment is negative or volatile (e.g., -0.47 to -0.57); model tends to overshoot into higher territory.
- Underestimate prices when sentiment is strongly negative (e.g., -0.70) or when recent prices are trending down; model fails to recognize mean reversion.
- Lag in correction: model often delays downward adjustments after negative sentiment, especially if recent prices are high.
- When sentiment turns positive (e.g., 0.37), model tends to overreact with upward bias, especially in early days of the forecast horizon.
- For 30-day forecasts, model consistently overestimates the first 5–7 days after a spike, then gradually converges — use a smoothing filter or decay factor for early horizon.
- If sentiment is consistently negative over 3–5 days, reduce forecast slope; model tends to ignore sentiment-driven corrections.
- When sentiment is neutral or mildly positive, model often overestimates by 1–2% — apply a 0.95 multiplier to forecast if sentiment > -0.20.
- Avoid extrapolating from recent high prices without sentiment context — if sentiment is negative, cap forecast at 1–2% below recent peak.
